gloss: recognize, regard; be or make strange, disguise; foreign, foreigner
summary: The root holds together knowing someone as one's own and finding him strange. The hiphil הִכִּיר is to look at and recognize, identify, distinguish, and so to acknowledge or take notice of, and “recognize faces” is to show partiality in judgment; the hithpael and niphal are to make oneself unrecognized, to disguise oneself or act as a stranger, and the piel to make a thing strange. The adjective נָכְרִי and the noun נֵכָר are the foreign and the foreigner, the man not known as kin, foreign gods and a foreign land. Joseph “recognized them, and made himself strange to them” (Gen 42:7), and Ruth asks why Boaz should “recognize” her, “and I a foreigner” (Rut 2:10); Arabic ʾankara “not know, deny” and tanakkara “disguise oneself”, and Akkadian nakru “foreign, enemy”, show the same two sides.

words.gloss: (hiphil) recognize, regard, acknowledge; (piel) make strange, misconstrue; (hithpael, niphal) disguise oneself, act as a stranger
words.summary: About fifty times. The hiphil (38) is the common stem: to look at a person or thing and know it, often negated, “he did not recognize him”. The piel, hithpael and niphal (11) turn the other way, to make a thing or oneself not known. The two meet in one verse: Joseph “recognized them (וַיַּכִּרֵם), and made himself strange (וַיִּתְנַכֵּר) to them” (Gen 42:7). BDB files the same tokens a second time as a denominative verb “treat as foreign” (n.do.ae); here they are one verb.

stems.gloss: recognize, identify; examine, distinguish; acknowledge, take notice of; (with פָּנִים) show partiality

senses.definition: To know a person or thing as the one it is, by sight, voice or a sign: a man in disguise, a brother after years, a friend disfigured by grief. Often with לֹא: he did not recognize him. Of the dead, “his place shall recognize him no more”.

evidence.note: “He did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like the hands of Esau his brother.”
“Joseph recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him.”
Saul recognized David's voice.
The Danites recognized the voice of the young Levite.
Obadiah recognized Elijah and fell on his face.
The king of Israel recognized the prophet once the bandage was off his eyes.
Job's friends saw him from afar “and did not recognize him”.
Ruth rose “before a man could recognize his neighbour”.
A form stood before Eliphaz, “and I could not recognize its appearance”.
Man is like grass: “the wind passes over it and it is gone, and its place recognizes it no more (וְלֹא־יַכִּירֶנּוּ עוֹד מְקוֹמוֹ)”.
“He shall return no more to his house, and his place shall recognize him no more.”
“Look on the right and see: there is no one who recognizes me.”

senses.definition: To look closely in order to know what a thing is or whose: the imperative הַכֶּר־נָא “examine, please”; to tell one sound from another; to perceive what lies behind a thing.

evidence.note: “We found this; הַכֶּר־נָא, is it your son's tunic or not?”
“He examined it (וַיַּכִּירָהּ) and said, It is my son's tunic.”
Tamar: “הַכֶּר־נָא, whose are these, the seal, the cords and the staff?”
“Judah identified them and said, She is more righteous than I.”
Jacob to Laban: “before our brothers identify what is yours with me, and take it.”
“The people could not distinguish (מַכִּירִים) the sound of the shout of joy from the sound of the people's weeping.”
“I perceived, and behold, God had not sent him.”
Their children “did not know how to speak Judean”.
All the people took note, and it was good in their eyes.
The rebels against the light “do not know its ways”.
They are familiar with the terrors of deep darkness.
God “knows their works” and overturns them in the night.

senses.gloss: acknowledge, own; take notice of, regard with favour
senses.definition: To know a person as one's own and treat him so: a father owning his firstborn, a man disowning his brothers, Yahweh regarding the exiles for good, the nations owning Israel's seed as blessed; and to take notice of one who has no claim.

evidence.note: “He shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the hated wife, by giving him a double portion.”
Levi “did not acknowledge his brothers, and did not know his sons”: parallel יָדַע.
“Abraham does not know us (לֹא יְדָעָנוּ), and Israel does not acknowledge us (לֹא יַכִּירָנוּ); you, Yahweh, are our father.”
“All who see them shall acknowledge them, that they are the seed Yahweh has blessed”; parallel נוֹדַע.
“Like these good figs, so I will regard the exiles of Judah for good.”
“Why have I found favour in your eyes, לְהַכִּירֵנִי, and I am a foreigner (נָכְרִיָּה)?”: to notice the one who is not known.
“Blessed be he who took notice of you.”
Those whom he acknowledges he will increase with glory.

senses.definition: In judgment, to know a face and favour it: to judge by who a man is, not by the cause. Always forbidden, beside נָשָׂא פָּנִים.

evidence.note: “לֹא־תַכִּירוּ פָנִים in judgment; hear the small as the great”.
“You shall not pervert judgment; you shall not recognize faces, nor take a bribe.”
“הַכֵּר־פָּנִים in judgment is not good.”
“To recognize faces is not good, and for a piece of bread a man will transgress.”

stems.gloss: regard; make strange, misconstrue, hand over as a stranger

senses.definition: As the hiphil: to take note of signs, and to favour the rich man's face over the poor.

evidence.note: God “does not lift the faces of princes, וְלֹא נִכַּר the rich before the poor”: parallel נָשָׂא פָּנִים.
“Have you not asked those who travel the road, and do you not recognize their signs?”

senses.gloss: make strange, estrange; misconstrue; give up as a stranger
senses.definition: To make a thing other than it is or not known for what it is: to make Yahweh's place a stranger's by burning incense in it to other gods; to misread Yahweh's judgment as the enemy's own work; to give a man up into another's hand.

evidence.note: “They have forsaken me וַיְנַכְּרוּ this place, and burned incense in it to other gods whom they did not know.”
“Lest their adversaries misconstrue (יְנַכְּרוּ), lest they say, Our hand is high, and Yahweh did not do all this.”
Saul: “God נִכַּר him into my hand”: has given him up, as one no longer his own; the Septuagint renders “sold”.

stems.gloss: act as a stranger, disguise oneself; make oneself known

senses.gloss: make oneself strange, act as a stranger; disguise oneself
senses.definition: To make oneself not known, by a changed manner or a changed appearance.

evidence.note: Joseph “recognized them, וַיִּתְנַכֵּר to them, and spoke harshly with them”.
Jeroboam's wife comes to Ahijah “disguising herself (מִתְנַכֵּרָה)”.
“Come in, wife of Jeroboam; why do you disguise yourself?”

senses.definition: To make oneself recognized, to show what one is.

evidence.note: “Even by his deeds a youth makes himself known (יִתְנַכֶּר), whether his work is pure and upright.”

senses.definition: To hide what one is behind one's speech.

evidence.note: “With his lips one who hates disguises himself (יִנָּכֵר), and within him he lays up deceit.”

senses.definition: To be known by sight.

evidence.note: The Nazirites, once brighter than snow: “their form is darker than soot; they are not recognized in the streets”.

evidence.locator: Gen.27.23; 37.33; 42.8; Deu.33.9; Isa.63.16, → ἐπέγνω; Gen.37.32; 38.25, הַכֶּר־נָא → ἐπίγνωθι; Deu.1.17; 16.19; 21.17; Rut.2.10; Ezr.3.13; Lam.4.8; ἐπιγινώσκω renders נָכַר about 30 times

evidence.note: On the road to Emmaus “their eyes were held, that they should not recognize (ἐπιγνῶναι) him”.
“Their eyes were opened, and they recognized (ἐπέγνωσαν) him.”
“By their fruits you will recognize them”: as a youth “makes himself known by his deeds” (Pro 20:11).

evidence.locator: Jer.19.4, וַיְנַכְּרוּ → ἀπηλλοτρίωσαν; Job.21.29; Gen.42.7, וַיִּתְנַכֵּר → ἠλλοτριοῦτο

evidence.note: “Alienated (ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι) from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise”.
“Alienated from the life of God.”
“You who were once alienated and enemies in your mind.”

parallels.note: “Know”: beside the hiphil, the same act of knowing a person as one's own.
“Lift the face”, favour a man: beside “recognize faces”.

phrases.gloss: recognize faces: show partiality in judgment

words.summary: Forty-five times: of a man or people not of Israel, often as a noun “a foreigner”; of the “foreign woman” of Proverbs and of the wives of Ezra 10; of one made a stranger to his own house; and of a thing strange in kind. Its constant parallel is זָר “stranger”, and it is set against אָח “brother”.

senses.definition: A man or people not of Israel, not a brother: one to whom interest may be charged and a debt not released, who may not be made king, who may yet come from a far land for Yahweh's name.

evidence.note: “The foreigner you may press, but what is yours with your brother your hand shall release.”
“You may not set over you a foreigner, who is not your brother.”
“To the foreigner you may lend at interest, but to your brother you shall not.”
What dies of itself may be given to the sojourner or sold to the foreigner.
“The foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, and comes from a far land for your name's sake.”
Ittai the Gittite: “you are a foreigner, and also an exile from your place”.
Ruth the Moabitess calls herself נָכְרִיָּה.
Gershom: “I have been a sojourner in a foreign land.”
A slave woman may not be sold to a foreign people.
“The foreigner who comes from a far land.”
“A city of a foreigner, which is not of the sons of Israel.”
“Strangers (זָרִים) carried off his wealth, and foreigners entered his gates.”
“Our inheritance is turned over to strangers, our houses to foreigners.”
God gives a man wealth, but a foreign man eats it.
“Lest strangers be filled with your strength, and your labours be in the house of a foreigner.”
“Let a stranger (זָר) praise you and not your own mouth, a foreigner and not your own lips”: another, not oneself.

senses.gloss: foreign woman, wife of another people
senses.definition: A woman of the nations taken as wife against the law, as Solomon's wives and those put away in Ezra's day; and in Proverbs the woman who is not one's own, whose smooth words lead to death, set beside the “strange woman” (אִשָּׁה זָרָה).

evidence.note: “King Solomon loved many foreign women … of the nations of which Yahweh said, You shall not go in to them.”
“Even him the foreign women caused to sin.”
“We have married foreign women of the peoples of the land.”
“To deliver you from the strange woman (אִשָּׁה זָרָה), from the foreign woman (נָכְרִיָּה) who makes her words smooth.”
“A foreign woman is a narrow well.”

senses.definition: One of the household treated or counted as not one's own.

evidence.note: Rachel and Leah: “Are we not counted by him as foreigners? For he has sold us.”
“I have become a stranger (מוּזָר) to my brothers, and a foreigner to my mother's sons.”
“My maidservants count me a stranger; I have become a foreigner in their eyes.”

senses.definition: Of a thing not of its proper kind: the foreign clothing of Judah's princes, a vine turned foreign, and Yahweh's own work of judgment on his people, strange to him.

evidence.note: “To do his work, strange (זָר) is his work, and to serve his service, foreign (נָכְרִיָּה) is his service.”
“I planted you a choice vine, wholly true seed; how have you turned into the degenerate shoots of a foreign vine?”
“All who clothe themselves in foreign clothing.”

greek.gloss: belonging to another; foreign, a stranger

evidence.note: “From their sons, or from strangers (ἀλλοτρίων)?”: the foreigner set against the son, as against the brother in Deu 15:3.
Abraham sojourned in the land of promise “as in a foreign (ἀλλοτρίαν) land”.
The sheep will not follow a stranger (ἀλλοτρίῳ), for they do not know the voice of strangers.

evidence.locator: 2Sa.15.19; Psa.69.9; Ecc.6.2, נָכְרִי → ξένος

evidence.note: “Strangers (ξένοι) to the covenants of the promise.”
“No longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints.”

parallels.note: “Stranger, other”: the constant partner, in the same line.

opposites.note: “Brother”: the foreigner is the one who is not a brother.

words.summary: Thirty-six times, almost always bound to another noun: בֶּן־נֵכָר “son of foreignness”, a foreigner; אֱלֹהֵי הַנֵּכָר “gods of the foreigner”, foreign gods; אַדְמַת נֵכָר “a foreign land”. The phrase בֶּן־נֵכָר is also listed in the entry for בֵּן (ben).

senses.definition: A man of another people: bought with silver into Abraham's house and circumcised, shut out of the Passover and the sanctuary while uncircumcised, yet to join himself to Yahweh, build Jerusalem's walls and serve Israel.

evidence.note: “Bought with silver from any son of foreignness, who is not of your seed.”
“No son of foreignness shall eat of it.”
“Sons of foreignness, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in my sanctuary.”
“Let not the son of foreignness who has joined himself to Yahweh say, Yahweh will surely separate me from his people.”
“Sons of foreignness shall build your walls.”
“Sons of foreignness cringe before me.”
“Whose mouth speaks vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of falsehood.”
“The seed of Israel separated themselves from all the sons of foreignness.”
“I cleansed them from everything foreign.”

senses.definition: The gods of the nations, which Israel was to put away: “gods of the foreigner”, “a god of foreignness”, against Yahweh who alone led Israel.

evidence.note: Jacob: “Put away the gods of the foreigner that are among you, and purify yourselves.”
“Put away the gods of the foreigner, and incline your heart to Yahweh the God of Israel.”
“Yahweh alone led him, and there was no foreign god (אֵל נֵכָר) with him.”
“There shall be no strange god (אֵל זָר) among you, and you shall not bow down to a foreign god (אֵל נֵכָר).”
“Why have they provoked me with their carved images, with foreign vanities?”
Judah “has married the daughter of a foreign god”.
Asa removed the foreign altars.

senses.definition: Ground not one's own, where Yahweh's song cannot be sung.

evidence.note: “How shall we sing Yahweh's song on foreign ground (אַדְמַת נֵכָר)?”
“As you served foreign gods in your land, so you shall serve strangers in a land not yours.”

evidence.locator: Exo.12.43; Ezk.44.7, 9; Isa.60.10, בֶּן־נֵכָר → ἀλλογενής

evidence.note: Of the Samaritan leper: “Were none found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner (ἀλλογενής)?”

parallels.note: “A strange god”: beside “a god of foreignness”.

phrases.gloss: gods of the foreigner: foreign gods

words.summary: Twice, in one passage: one known to the priests, from whom they received the silver. The noun is formed on the hiphil's “recognize”: the one a man knows.

senses.definition: A man known to another, here the donors each priest knew.

evidence.note: “Let the priests take for themselves, each from his acquaintance (מַכָּרוֹ).”

words.summary: Twice, as a parallel of אֵיד “calamity”. Arabic nakrāʾ “calamity, severity of fortune” is the same word; how it joins the root's “strange, unknown” is not shown by the verses (perhaps the hostile, as Akkadian nakru “enemy”).

senses.definition: The evil day that falls on a man or a people.

evidence.note: “Is not calamity (אֵיד) for the unrighteous, and disaster (נֵכֶר) for the workers of iniquity?”
“Do not gaze on the day of your brother, on the day of his misfortune (נָכְרוֹ)”; the next verse has “the day of their calamity (אֵידָם)”.

words.summary: Once: the hiphil's verbal noun, what is recognized of a face, its look.

senses.definition: What can be read in a face: here its look testifies against the wicked.

evidence.note: “The look of their faces (הַכָּרַת פְּנֵיהֶם) testifies against them, and they declare their sin like Sodom.”

words.summary: Only in בֵּית נְכֹתֹה, Hezekiah's treasure house shown to the envoys of Babylon (2Ki 20:13; Isa 39:2), where the context lists silver, gold, spices and oil. It answers Akkadian bīt nakkamti (also written nakkanti) “treasure house”, from which it is most likely borrowed; no tie to the root's “recognize, foreign” is known.

senses.definition: A king's stored wealth; בֵּית נְכֹת is the treasure house.

evidence.note: “He showed them all his treasure house (בֵּית נְכֹתֹה), the silver and the gold and the spices and the good oil.”
The same account, בֵּית נְכֹתוֹ.

words.summary: The Peshitta's word of the root, twenty-one times in the New Testament, for ἀλλότριος, ἀλλογενής, ἀλλόφυλος, ξένος and ἀπαλλοτριόω: the stranger set against the son, the foreigner, and what is strange or alien.

senses.gloss: a stranger, foreigner, not a son
senses.definition: One not of the family or the people: the strangers against the sons, the Samaritan, the Gentile, the stranger whose voice the sheep do not know, a foreign land.

evidence.note: “From their sons, or מֵנ נֻוכֿרָיֵא?”
“From strangers.” “Then the sons are free.”
“If you are without discipline … you are נֻוכֿרָיֵא and not sons.”
“This one who is from a foreign people” (ἀλλογενής).
Peter: unlawful for a Jew to join himself to a foreign man (ἀλλοφύλῳ).
“After a stranger they will not go … for they do not know the voice of the stranger”: the stranger is the one not known.
“Are you alone a stranger from Jerusalem?”
Abraham's seed would sojourn “in a foreign land”.
Abraham sojourned in the land promised him “as in a foreign one (אַיכֿ דַּבֿנֻוכֿרָיתָּא)”.
“Strangers from the commonwealth of Israel.”
The foreigners living at Athens.

senses.definition: Of a thing not one's own or not familiar: foreign gods, strange words and teaching, another's foundation, another's sins, a strange trial, a foreign tongue.

evidence.note: “He proclaims foreign gods (אַלָהֵא נֻוכֿרָיֵא).”
“You bring strange things to our ears.”
“Do not be carried away by various and strange teachings.”
“That I might not build on a foundation not my own.”
“Do not share in the sins of others.”
“As though something strange were happening to you.”
“With a foreign speech and another tongue I will speak to this people”, after Isa 28:11.

senses.definition: Made strangers, alienated from God and his life.

evidence.note: “Estranged from the life of God, because of the ignorance in them.”
“You who were once estranged and enemies in your thoughts.”

cognates.gloss: not know, be unacquainted with, ignore; deny, disown; disapprove; (nakira) ignorance; (munkar) unknown; disapproved, evil
cognates.note: The same act as the Hebrew hiphil turned the other way: where הִכִּיר is to know a person again and own him, ʾankara is to fail to know him or to disown him, the opposite of ʿarafa “know”. Its “unknown” (munkar, nakira) is the Hebrew's foreigner, the man not known as one's own. Lane's ʾistinkār, inquiring into a thing one finds strange, is close to the hiphil's “examine”.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2849, art. نكر, أنكره (n40515)
evidence.note: “He ignored, was ignorant of, did not know, failed to know, or [rather] was unacquainted with, it … or him”; contr. of عَرَفَهُ.
“Ignorance … contr. of مَعْرِفَةٌ”; “the inquiring respecting … a thing … which one disapproves”.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2850, art. نكر, مُنْكَرٌ (n40531)
evidence.note: “Ignored, or unknown … denied, or disacknowledged … deemed strange”.

cognates.gloss: change a thing so that it is not known, disguise it; (tanakkara) disguise oneself; become changed in countenance, meet one morosely
cognates.note: The Hebrew hithpael and niphal exactly: Jeroboam's wife disguising herself (1Ki 14:5), and Joseph making himself strange and speaking harshly (Gen 42:7), as tanakkara li “he met me morosely, changed in countenance so that I did not know him”. Form II, changing a thing so it is not known, matches the piel's making Yahweh's place strange (Jer 19:4).

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2849, art. نكر, نكّره (n40513)
evidence.note: “He changed, or altered, him or it, to an unknown state, so as not to be known; [he disguised him or it.]”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2850, art. نكر, تنكّر (n40516)
evidence.note: “He disguised himself … became changed or altered in countenance by anger so that he who saw him did not know him … met me in a morose manner.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2851, art. نكر, خَرَجَ مُتَنَكِّرًا (n40533)
evidence.note: “He went forth disguised.”

cognates.gloss: a calamity; severity of fortune; something evil, abominable
cognates.note: The Hebrew נֶכֶר “calamity” of Job 31:3 and Oba 1:12.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2850, art. نكر, نَكْرَآءُ (n40527)
evidence.note: “A calamity: rigour, or severity, of fortune.”

cognates.gloss: (nakru) foreign, strange; foreigner, stranger, enemy; (nakāru) be or become different, changed, estranged, hostile; alter, remove; (nukurtu) hostility
cognates.note: Thousands of times in Akkadian: the foreigner is the enemy, and the verb is to become other, estranged. The Hebrew foreigner and the piel's making a place strange share it; the hostility is not in the Hebrew words for “foreign”, though perhaps behind נֶכֶר “disaster”.

evidence.locator: armep x000005380, nakru [enemy] N: enemy; foreign; foreigner; stranger
armep x000013610, nakru [strange] AJ: enemy; foreign; hostile; strange
armep x000013920, nakāru [be(come) different] V: alienate; alter; be(come) different; be(come) estranged; be(come) hostile
armep x000049430, nukurtu [enmity] N

cognates.note: Hebrew בֵּית נְכֹת answers bīt nakkamti, the Assyrian and Babylonian treasure house, with the m assimilated as in the spelling nakkanti. The word is from Akkadian nakāmu “heap up”, not from נכר; it was most likely borrowed in the Assyrian period, the time of Hezekiah.

evidence.locator: armep x000028620, nakkamtu [treasure] N: reserve; storehouse; treasure; treasury; forms nakkamti, nakkanti, nakkantu

cognates.gloss: (aphel) recognize, know; (ithpaal) be distinguishable; (pael) make strange, remove
cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic, in the Targums and Talmud, with both sides of the Hebrew verb: the Targum of Gen 38:25 renders Tamar's הַכֶּר־נָא with the aphel, and the pael is to make a thing strange and put it away.

evidence.locator: s.v. נְכַר (ch.), citing Targ. Y. I Gen. XXXVIII, 25 sq. (Af. אַכֵּר, recognize); B. Kam. 5a, 97a (Ithpa., be distinguishable); Sabb. 82b (Pa., make strange, remove)

cognates.note: The Targums' word for the Hebrew נָכְרִי, as at Deu 17:15.

evidence.locator: s.v. נוּכְרָא, citing Targ. Prov. VI, 1; Targ. O. Deut. XVII, 15

cognates.note: Syriac; the adjective is the Peshitta's, used for ἀλλότριος and its kin (see its word in this entry). SEDRA lists a verb “repudiate” with no Peshitta New Testament occurrence.

evidence.locator: root 1179 נכר; lexemes 1977 נוכריא (strange; foreign; alien), 1978 נכר (repudiate)

cognates.gloss: be strange, alien; (nakir) stranger, foreign, strange
cognates.note: Ge'ez keeps the root's “strange, foreign”, as the Hebrew נָכְרִי.

evidence.locator: s.v. nakara

cognates.note: Given as Ugaritic in Wiktionary's Arabic and Ugaritic entries; not yet checked in a Ugaritic dictionary.

evidence.locator: Ugaritic 𐎐𐎋𐎗; Arabic نكر, etymology
evidence.note: “foreigner, alien”; compares Hebrew נָכְרִי.

doctrine.statement: The law set the foreigner apart from the brother: he could not be king (Deu 17:15), and no son of foreignness, uncircumcised, could eat the Passover or enter the sanctuary (Exo 12:43; Ezk 44:7, 9). Yet Abraham's house took in the son of foreignness bought with silver and circumcised him (Gen 17:12, 27); Solomon prayed that Yahweh would hear “the foreigner who is not of your people Israel” who comes for his name's sake, “that all the peoples of the earth may know your name” (1Ki 8:41–43); Boaz took notice of Ruth, who called herself a foreigner, because she had come to trust under the wings of the God of Israel (Rut 2:10, 12); and Isaiah tells the son of foreignness who joins himself to Yahweh, loves his name and holds his covenant, not to say “Yahweh will separate me from his people”, for “my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples” (Isa 56:3, 6–7). Paul writes to Gentile believers that they were once “alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise, having no hope and without God in the world”, but are now “no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints” (Eph 2:12, 19), and “if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal 3:29). From the verses: the foreigner is not shut out by birth but by being outside the covenant; joined to Yahweh and his covenant, he shares Israel's hope, which is the promise made to Abraham.

Yahweh said to Abraham, “All the land which you see, to you I will give it, and to your seed for ever” (Gen 13:15), and “I will give to you and to your seed after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession” (Gen 17:8). Stephen says that God “gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's breadth, but promised to give it to him for a possession, and to his seed after him” (Act 7:5). Hebrews says that by faith Abraham “sojourned in the land of promise as in a foreign land (Peshitta נֻוכֿרָיתָּא), dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise” (Heb 11:9), that these all “died in faith, not having received the promises” (Heb 11:13), and that they have not yet received them, “God having provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect” (Heb 11:39–40). From the verses: Abraham lived in the promised land as a foreigner and died without owning it; the promise to him personally is still to be fulfilled, when he and the faithful are made perfect together at the resurrection.

Jacob told his house, “Put away the gods of the foreigner that are among you” (Gen 35:2), and Joshua and Samuel repeated it to Israel, “put away the gods of the foreigner … and incline your heart to Yahweh the God of Israel”, “and serve him only” (Jos 24:23; 1Sa 7:3). Moses sang, “Yahweh alone led him, and there was no foreign god with him” (Deu 32:12), and the psalm sets it as the first word of the covenant: “there shall be no strange god among you, and you shall not bow down to a foreign god; I am Yahweh your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (Psa 81:10–11). Malachi calls marriage to the daughter of a foreign god a profaning of Yahweh's holiness (Mal 2:11). Paul writes, “we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no God but one … to us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things” (1Co 8:4, 6), as Moses said, “Hear, O Israel: Yahweh our God, Yahweh is one” (Deu 6:4). From the verses: the gods of the nations are “foreign” to Israel because Yahweh alone brought Israel out and led it; there is one God, the Father, and no other to be served beside him.

Of man in death the hiphil says, “his place shall recognize him no more”: “as the cloud is consumed and vanishes, so he who goes down to the grave (שְׁאוֹל) shall not come up; he shall return no more to his house, and his place shall know him no more” (Job 7:9–10); “as for man, his days are as grass … the wind passes over it and it is gone, and its place knows it no more” (Psa 103:15–16). The same psalm sets against this “the steadfast love of Yahweh from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him” (Psa 103:17), and Job, who says “man lies down and does not rise, till the heavens are no more”, asks Yahweh to hide him in the grave and appoint a time to remember him: “you will call, and I will answer you” (Job 14:12–15). From the verses: death ends a man's whole life and presence on earth, with nothing of him left to be known there; his hope is that Yahweh will remember him and call him back.

note: BDB files the verb twice, as נָכַר “regard, recognize” (n.dn.aa) and a denominative נכר “treat as foreign” (n.do.ae), over the same 49 tokens; the entry names only n.dn.aa, as the README says for one set of occurrences under two keys. The 0-token cross-reference keys e.bi.ab (הַכָּרַת) and m.by.ah (מַכָּר) are left unnamed. The root has none of the merged letters, so no `sounds`. Open questions: (1) The Arabic simple verb is “not know, disown” where the Hebrew hiphil is “recognize, own”; both are the one act of knowing a person as one's own or not, and ar-nakira is named on the hiphil on that ground. Check whether the reviewer accepts it. (2) נְכֹת is kept here because BDB files it under this spelling, but it is most likely an Akkadian loan (bīt nakkamti, from nakāmu); decide whether it should have an entry of its own. 1Sa 23:7 נִכַּר “God has handed him over” is read as the piel “give up as a stranger”; the Septuagint has πιπράσκω “sell” (as if מָכַר). Check Ge'ez in Leslau 1987 (page) and Dillmann 1865 col., and Ugaritic nkr in DULAT; both cited here only by headword or from Wiktionary. Peshitta: SEDRA lexeme 1978 נכר “repudiate” has no New Testament occurrence. The phrase בֶּן־נֵכָר is also in ben.json (בֵּן) as a phrase; left there. No personal name in TIPNR is formed from this root (Machir is from מכר).
